opus-5.5.text:
I think object manipulation is just the most visible piece of it. When we watch people interact with the world, there's a lot more information than "here's how you grasp a mug." There's intent, there's sequencing, there's how people recover when something goes wrong, and there's how they coordinate with other people. All of that is embedded in everyday human activity, and it's exactly the kind of knowledge that's really hard to hand-engineer into a robot.

One area I'm excited about is learning task structure and long-horizon reasoning. If you look at someone cooking a meal or tidying up a room, the interesting part isn't any single motion. It's how they break the task into steps, what order they choose, and how they adapt when the environment doesn't cooperate. Human data gives us a window into that higher-level decision-making, and I think robots can learn useful priors from it even when their bodies look very different from ours.

Another piece is interaction with people themselves. If robots are going to work in homes, hospitals, or warehouses alongside humans, they need to understand things like handovers, turn-taking, and how to anticipate what a person is about to do. You can't get that from robot-only data collected in a lab. You need to observe how humans actually behave around each other and around shared spaces.

And then there's the scaling argument. Robot data is expensive. You need hardware, teleoperators, and resets, and it grows slowly. Human data, especially with wearable sensors, egocentric video, or lightweight capture devices, can be collected much more naturally and at much larger scale. So part of my view is practical: if we want robots that generalize, we have to tap into the data source that already exists in abundance, which is people living their lives.

The challenge, of course, is the embodiment gap. Humans have different hands, different kinematics, different sensing. So the research question becomes: what is transferable? I'd argue the things that transfer best are often the more abstract ones, such as goals, object affordances, task decomposition, and where to pay attention, rather than exact joint trajectories. A lot of our work is about finding the right representation so that robots can absorb what's useful from human behavior and fill in the low-level details with their own experience.

So my short answer is that human interaction data is less about copying motions and more about inheriting a huge amount of common-sense knowledge about how the physical and social world works. That's what I think will make robots genuinely useful outside of narrow, structured settings.

r001.rationale: The response says robots need observations of how humans behave around each other, but does not state that human–human interactions are currently the only source of interaction data for teaching robots to interact with people.

r002.rationale: It discusses robots interacting with people and gives examples such as handovers and turn-taking, but does not identify human–robot interaction as a major unexplored area.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think human interaction data is probably the most underrated resource we have in robot learning right now, and the reason is that it captures something that pure object manipulation data just can't. When you watch a person do a task, you're not only seeing where their hand goes and how they grasp a cup. You're seeing how they decompose a long-horizon activity into steps, how they recover when something goes wrong, how they sequence things in a kitchen, how they adapt when the environment isn't quite what they expected. That structure, the procedural and compositional knowledge, is what robots are really missing.

My view is that there are kind of two layers to what a robot needs to learn. There's the low-level sensorimotor layer, the actual contact-rich control, and honestly that's hard to get from human video because the embodiment gap is real. A human hand and a robot gripper are just different, and the physics of contact doesn't transfer cleanly. But then there's this higher layer, the task-level understanding, the planning, the affordances, the "what should I do next and why." And for that layer, human data is incredibly rich and incredibly abundant. There's orders of magnitude more human activity video in the world than there will ever be robot teleoperation data.

So the way we've been thinking about it in my group is, how do you use human interaction data to learn the structure of tasks, the subgoals, the spatial and temporal relationships between actions, and then ground that into robot-specific skills that you learn from a much smaller amount of robot data. Human data tells you what to do; robot data tells you how to do it on this particular body.

The other thing I'd add is that human interaction data goes beyond manipulation in a social sense too. Robots that work in homes or hospitals need to understand people, how they move through space, when they're about to hand you something, what their intent is. You can't learn that from a robot pushing blocks on a table. You learn it from watching humans interact with each other and with their environment. So I really see it as the bridge between robots that can do isolated skills in a lab and robots that can actually operate in the messy, human-centered world.

r002.rationale: The response discusses social understanding and human-centered settings, but does not identify human–robot interaction as a major unexplored area in human data for robot learning.

astra-6.text:
I think human interaction data is important because object manipulation is only one part of what a robot needs to do around people. It also needs to understand what someone is trying to accomplish, when to help, and when to ask for clarification. Those are things you don’t necessarily learn from watching a successful grasp.

Imagine a robot helping you prepare a meal. It’s not just picking up ingredients. It needs to coordinate with you: Are you reaching for something? Are you waiting for the robot? Did your plan change? Human interaction data can give us examples of that coordination, including how people recover when they misunderstand each other.

The challenge is figuring out what to learn from those examples. We don’t want a robot to simply imitate a person’s movements. We want it to learn how its actions affect the other person and use their feedback to adapt. That moves us toward robots that can participate in a shared task, rather than just execute an isolated skill.

sol-6.1.text:
I think human interaction data is important because manipulating an object is only one part of acting in the world. If a robot is helping someone, it also needs to understand what that person is trying to do, when to offer help, and when to wait. Those decisions depend on the interaction, not just on recognizing objects or predicting their motion.

Take handing someone a tool. The robot needs to choose a useful orientation, but it also needs to recognize whether the person is ready to receive it and respond if they change their mind. Human interaction data can provide examples of that coordination—how people use gaze, gestures, language, and physical actions together.

The challenge is that observing an interaction doesn’t necessarily reveal the intention behind it. So I see demonstrations and videos as a starting point, complemented by robots interacting with people and learning from feedback. The goal is to teach robots to adapt to a person as the situation unfolds.
